title: Hezekiah Trusts the LORD and Assyria Mocks
summary: Hezekiah becomes king of Judah and does what his father Ahaz would not: he removes the high places, breaks up the bronze snake Moses made, trusts the LORD, and rebels against Assyria. After a brief retelling of Samaria's fall, Sennacherib invades Judah, takes its fortified cities, and extracts a heavy tribute, then sends his officials to Jerusalem anyway. The Rabshakeh stands outside the wall and mocks Hezekiah's trust in the LORD, in Hebrew, so that the people can hear.
story: The book has just recounted the end of the northern kingdom (chapter 17), and Judah now faces the same empire. Ahaz had met the Assyrian threat by becoming Assyria's servant (chapter 16). His son Hezekiah does the opposite, and the narrator praises him more highly than any king since David: none was like him in trusting the LORD (verse 5). Verses 9-12 repeat the fall of Samaria on purpose, to set Hezekiah's story in its shadow. The question of chapters 18 and 19 is the one the Rabshakeh asks in verse 19: what is the basis of this confidence? Samaria trusted other gods and fell. Will Jerusalem, trusting the LORD, fare differently? Chapters 18 to 20 are also found, with small differences, in Isaiah 36 to 39.
historical:
Hezekiah's dates are one of the famous puzzles of biblical chronology. Verse 1 places his accession around 727 BC (in Hoshea's third year), but verse 13 puts Sennacherib's invasion, securely dated to 701 BC, in his fourteenth year, which would place his accession around 715 BC. Scholars resolve this in different ways, most often by proposing a co-regency with Ahaz or by preferring one of the two synchronisms. He died around 686 BC.

Sennacherib ruled Assyria from 705 to 681 BC. When he came to the throne, several western vassals, Hezekiah among them, stopped paying tribute, and in 701 BC he marched west. His own annals, preserved on clay prisms, describe the campaign: he claims to have taken forty-six of Hezekiah's fortified cities, deported many people, and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage, and he lists a tribute that included thirty talents of gold, the same figure as verse 14 (his figure for silver is higher). Notably, the annals do not claim that Jerusalem was taken. Sennacherib had the siege of Lachish, Judah's second city, carved in stone reliefs for his palace at Nineveh, and excavations at Lachish have uncovered the Assyrian siege ramp and a destruction layer from this campaign. Hezekiah's preparations for a siege, including the water tunnel mentioned in 20:20, are also known from archaeology.
cultural:
The three Assyrian officials carry titles, not personal names: the Tartan was the army's commander in chief, the Rabsaris a senior court official, and the Rabshakeh (literally chief cupbearer) a high officer who here acts as spokesman. Speaking to a besieged city's people over the heads of its leaders was a known tactic of psychological war. Aramaic was the international language of diplomacy in the Assyrian empire, understood by officials but not by ordinary Judeans, which is why Hezekiah's men ask the Rabshakeh to use it and why he refuses.

His speech is shrewd. He knows about Judah's hope in Egypt and mocks it as a splintered reed. He knows that Hezekiah has closed the high places and centralized worship in Jerusalem, and he twists that reform into an offense against the LORD. He even claims the LORD sent him, which may reflect knowledge of prophets like Isaiah, who had called Assyria the rod of God's anger (Isaiah 10:5). The picture in verses 31-32 of every man under his own vine and fig tree was Israel's traditional image of peace (1 Kings 4:25; Micah 4:4); the Rabshakeh offers it as the reward for surrender, followed by deportation to a land like their own. The bronze snake of verse 4 was the one Moses made in the wilderness, which healed those who looked at it (Numbers 21:8-9); over time it had become an object of worship.
literary: The chapter has two parts. Verses 1-12 are the regnal introduction, with the highest praise given any king in Kings and a reprise of Samaria's fall as a foil. Verses 13-37 begin a long narrative that runs through chapter 19. Most of it is speech, and the key word is trust (the Hebrew root batach), which occurs again and again: Hezekiah trusted in the LORD (verse 5), and the Rabshakeh asks what he is trusting in (verses 19-22, 30). The speech is built as a series of taunts that close off every hope: not strategy, not Egypt, not the LORD, not Hezekiah, not any god of any nation. Its final question, how can the LORD deliver Jerusalem (verse 35), puts the LORD on the same level as the gods of Hamath and Arpad. The chapter ends in silence, with the people obeying the king's order not to answer, and the officials tearing their clothes.

outline.t: The Rabshakeh: what are you trusting in?
The appeal to the people on the wall

doctrines.note: Trust is the chapter's theme. Hezekiah's defining trait is that he trusted the LORD, and the enemy's whole strategy is to break that trust. The chapter shows that faith is tested exactly at the point where it seems least reasonable.
Hezekiah destroys even the bronze snake Moses made, because people had begun burning incense to it. A good gift of God becomes an idol when it is worshiped instead of the God who gave it.

The Rabshakeh treats the LORD as one local god among many. The rest of the story (chapter 19) will answer that claim. The LORD is not a god of one land who can be compared with others; he is the living God.

words.note: Batach, to trust, to feel secure in, to rely on. It is the chapter's key word, occurring in verse 5 and then repeatedly in the Rabshakeh's speech. The same verb is common in the Psalms for trust in God. The whole conflict turns on it: the question is not whether Judah trusts but in whom.

Nehushtan, the name given to Moses' bronze snake. It sounds like the Hebrew words for bronze (nechoshet) and snake (nachash), so it may mean something like the bronze thing or bronze snake. Some interpreters take the naming as Hezekiah's dismissive label: it's only a piece of bronze.

Natsal, to snatch away, rescue, or deliver. The Rabshakeh uses it nine times in his speech, insisting that no god has delivered his land from Assyria's hand. The verb frames the question the next chapter answers.

christ: Jesus himself referred to the bronze snake that Hezekiah destroyed. In John 3:14-15 he said that as Moses lifted up the snake in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may have eternal life. The snake had been God's means of healing, and when it became an idol Hezekiah was right to break it; what it pointed to was never the bronze but God's own provision of life for the dying, which the New Testament finds fulfilled in the cross. The chapter's larger theme also looks forward. Hezekiah trusted the LORD when the world's greatest power mocked that trust as empty. The Gospels show Jesus mocked in the same terms, told to let God rescue him if God wanted him (Matthew 27:43), and trusting the Father through death to resurrection.

hard.q: Why does Hezekiah, who trusted the LORD, pay tribute and strip the temple doors?
hard.a:
Verses 14-16 are striking right after the praise of verses 5-7. Hezekiah admits he has done wrong, pays an enormous sum, and strips even the gold he had put on the temple doors. Some readers see this as a lapse of faith, much like Ahaz's payment to Tiglath-pileser, and note that it didn't work: the Assyrians came to Jerusalem anyway. Others read it as a responsible king's attempt to spare his people when his land was already overrun, not a denial of trust in the LORD.

The narrator doesn't comment, which leaves both readings possible. What the story does show is that paying off the empire did not buy safety. The rescue of Jerusalem in chapter 19 comes not from Hezekiah's payment but from his prayer, which suggests that the deeper answer to the Rabshakeh's question was still ahead of him.

questions: Hezekiah broke up a bronze snake that had once been a genuine means of God's healing. What good things in your life or church are in danger of receiving the trust that belongs to God?
The Rabshakeh's speech works by closing off every hope one by one. How do you answer the voices, inside or outside you, that insist your trust in God is foolish?
Hezekiah told the people not to answer. When is silence the wisest response to mockery?
